issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the abstract, methods, and results are based on a randomized/dummy Qualtrics dataset rather than real participant data. This makes all reported empirical findings invalid as evidence, and any inferential statistics, conclusions, and replication claims are uninterpretable. A manuscript reporting simulated placeholder results cannot support scientific claims about replication or extension.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.description: The methods/results again confirm that analyses were conducted on generated responses rather than observed data. This is fatal to internal validity and means no replication has actually been performed.
issues.quote: [IMPORTANT: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.]

issues.subcategory: abstract reports placeholder results as real
issues.description: Despite the explicit note that results are simulated, the abstract presents them in standard empirical language ('found no empirical support', 'Results have supported'). This is misleading and could easily be interpreted as actual study findings.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the “perceived impact of donation” as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis...

issues.description: The manuscript frames itself as a replication and extension, but no actual data collection appears to have occurred. A protocol or preregistration manuscript should not be written as if a replication has been executed and evaluated.
issues.quote: In this pre-registered study, we conducted a replication of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic’s (2007) Studies 1 and 3

issues.description: The authors merge Studies 1 and 3 into a single experiment and also apply the intervention to the joint condition, which did not exist in the original design. This substantially alters the experimental structure and undermines the claim of a close/direct replication. Such redesign changes the estimands, interactions, and interpretation.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect... The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition

issues.description: The manuscript labels the study as a 'close to very close replication' despite numerous major deviations: online MTurk sample instead of in-person university sample, hypothetical donation instead of real donation, merged studies, added conditions, updated materials, no pre-survey compensation, and added measures. This classification overstates methodological similarity.
issues.quote: Table 7 summarizes the current replication as a "close to very close replication".

issues.description: The procedures state that participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions. This directly contradicts experimental random assignment and introduces severe selection bias/confounding. It invalidates causal inference regarding intervention and identifiability effects.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The manuscript describes the experiment as a within-subject design, but the reported condition cell sample sizes sum to the total N and appear to reflect independent groups. The original studies were between-subjects. This unresolved inconsistency prevents understanding of the actual design and appropriate analysis.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables

issues.subcategory: analysis inconsistent with claimed within-subject design
issues.description: If the study were truly within-subject, standard between-subject two-way ANOVA with residual df=994 and cell Ns would be inappropriate; repeated-measures or mixed models would be required, with participant-level dependencies modeled. The reported analyses strongly suggest a between-subject design. This mismatch calls into question all statistical tests.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.description: The participant section reports generated Qualtrics responses with an implausible age distribution but does not describe any actual recruitment frame or sample characteristics. This prevents evaluation of sample comparability and external validity.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.description: The reported age distribution (mean 67.8, SD 30.1, range 18-120) is implausible for an MTurk/online psychology sample and signals that these are arbitrary generated values rather than realistic data. This further emphasizes that the statistical outputs are meaningless placeholders.
issues.quote: Median age (years) | 68 ... Average age (years) | 67.8 ... Age range (years) | 18-120

issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly specify the intended actual recruitment source, inclusion criteria, compensation, exclusion thresholds, or target sample after exclusions in a coherent final protocol. It alternates between generated data and future MTurk data.
issues.quote: Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform

issues.description: Exclusions are mentioned but operational details are omitted: what constitutes prior knowledge, what attention checks were used, whether exclusions were preregistered, and how many cases were excluded. This prevents reproducibility and can affect results materially.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.subcategory: power analysis not reported in manuscript
issues.description: The manuscript claims sample size was determined by power analysis but provides no actual assumptions, target effect, alpha, desired power, design specification, or resulting minimum N in the manuscript itself. Referring readers to a supplement is insufficient for key design justification, especially given the major redesign from the original.
issues.quote: The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.subcategory: replication target changed by hypothetical donation
issues.description: The original study involved real donations from actual money participants received; this study uses imaginary donations from $0 to $5. Hypothetical donation can differ substantially from incentivized behavior, affecting construct validity and comparability to the original effect.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.subcategory: replication target changed by updated stimuli
issues.description: The authors replace the original victim information with updated material from Save the Children. While understandable, this changes the emotional salience and informational content of the manipulation, potentially altering the effect and reducing direct comparability.
issues.quote: We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.description: The explicit intervention is central to the hypothesis, but the exact wording/materials are not described in the manuscript. Without the manipulation text, readers cannot assess fidelity to the original, strength of manipulation, or replicability.
issues.quote: participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims

issues.description: There is no reported manipulation check for whether participants understood or engaged with the explicit intervention or whether the joint condition implicitly induced analytic thinking. Without such checks, null or altered effects are difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: The victim statistics was believed to eliminate the identifiable victim effect implicitly in the joint condition

issues.subcategory: combining explicit and implicit manipulations creates confounds
issues.description: By adding intervention to the joint condition, the design mixes explicit and implicit debiasing mechanisms in a way not present in the original studies. This confounds interpretation of identifiability, intervention, and their interaction because the joint condition is no longer a pure implicit manipulation.
issues.quote: The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: ordinal outcome analyzed with ANOVA without justification
issues.description: Donation is bounded from $0 to $5 and apparently measured in integer dollar amounts. The original study reportedly used ordered probit regression, but the replication drops it without rationale and relies on ANOVA/t tests. For bounded ordinal/count-like outcomes, ANOVA assumptions may be questionable.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.subcategory: analytic deviations from original not justified
issues.description: The manuscript changes the main analyses from the original, including not using ordered probit and adding different post-hoc comparisons. Such deviations should be strongly justified, especially in a replication attempting comparability.
issues.quote: This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript conducts many ANOVAs and post-hoc tests across multiple feeling variables, interactions, and correlations. There is no comprehensive multiple-comparison control strategy beyond selective Bonferroni pairwise tests. This inflates Type I error, particularly for the extension and segregated feelings analyses.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA ... on segregated affective reactions

issues.description: The manuscript states post-hoc tests are conditional on significant omnibus effects in some places, but proceeds inconsistently. Moreover, pairwise testing after a marginal or small omnibus effect without clear familywise error control can produce misleading significance claims.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: effect size interpretation inconsistent with results
issues.description: The reported significant effects have extremely small eta-squared values (e.g., ηp2=.007, .008), yet are discussed substantively as supported effects. This is likely driven by the large simulated N and should be interpreted cautiously; practical significance is negligible.

issues.subcategory: incorrect interpretation of direction of effect
issues.description: The post-hoc results indicate higher donation in the statistical victim condition than the identifiable victim condition, which is the reverse of the identifiable victim effect. Yet the manuscript describes the identifiability effect as supported without adequately emphasizing that it is opposite in direction to the original phenomenon.
issues.quote: meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: claims of support despite opposite-direction finding
issues.description: Because the effect is opposite the original prediction, describing the identifiability main effect as 'supported' is conceptually misleading. A replication should evaluate direction and compatibility with the original effect, not just significance.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.

issues.subcategory: contrast test not aligned with redesigned study
issues.description: The contrast comparing identifiable/no intervention against all other five cells is inherited from the original but becomes conceptually arbitrary once the design is expanded to six conditions including joint/intervention and joint/no intervention. Pooling heterogeneous conditions can obscure meaningful structure and does not correspond to a preregistered theoretically coherent contrast as described here.
issues.quote: contrast the mean difference of identifiable/no intervention on donation with the combination of 5 conditions

issues.description: The manuscript refers to aggregated feelings but never specifies exactly how items were combined, whether scales were standardized, whether reverse coding was needed, or whether internal consistency justified aggregation. Without this, the construct and analysis are opaque.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: no reliability statistics for multi-item measures
issues.description: There is no report of internal consistency (e.g., alpha/omega) for the aggregated feelings scale or justification for combining items. This is essential for evaluating measurement quality.
issues.quote: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.subcategory: extension hypothesis mismatched with cited literature
issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable versus statistical victims, but the literature review itself notes mixed evidence and some null findings. The rationale is not sufficiently developed, especially since the original discussion of efficacy/proportion dominance may not map directly onto this modified design.
issues.quote: It is hypothesized that people generally perceive a stronger impact of donation towards an identified victim than unidentified statistical victims.

issues.subcategory: extension conclusion not supported by stated hypothesis
issues.description: The significant post-hoc finding is between statistical and joint conditions, not identifiable and statistical conditions as hypothesized. Therefore the extension hypothesis is not supported, yet the abstract and text imply support.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: post-hoc result does not test hypothesis 6 directly
issues.description: Hypothesis 6 predicted identifiable > statistical on perceived impact. The reported significant pairwise difference is statistical vs joint; identifiable vs statistical is null. Thus the claimed support is incorrect.
issues.quote: Identifiable VS Statistical ... pBonferroni 1.000 ... Statistical VS Joint ... .041*

issues.description: For the significant perceived impact effect and other feeling variables, means and SDs by condition are not fully tabulated in the manuscript, making interpretation and checking of direction difficult.
issues.quote: We conducted post-hoc tests to further study the difference of identifiability on the perceived impact of donation.

issues.description: The manuscript reports 95% CIs for ANOVA effect sizes but does not specify whether these are for partial eta-squared, and in several places confidence intervals appear mechanically narrow and uninformative. Methods for CI calculation are not adequately explained.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: no exact p-values for original study effects
issues.description: The manuscript reproduces original results only as '<.05' or '<.01', limiting comparison and effect-size reconstruction transparency. If the purpose is replication evaluation, exact statistics from the target article or clear derivations should be provided when possible.
issues.quote: Original study | 1 | 6.75 | <.05* | .06

issues.subcategory: improper comparison of original and replication effects
issues.description: Replication evaluation is said to compare the replication effect to the original effect d=0.48, but the main replication analyses use ANOVA with three-level identifiability and altered design. A direct effect-size comparison is not straightforward and is not properly implemented in the reported results.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.description: The 'joint condition' is treated as identifiable victim with statistics, but that is not equivalent to simply adding identifiability level. It represents a qualitatively different evaluative context that may invoke comparison processes. Treating identifiability as a simple 3-level factor may obscure distinct psychological mechanisms.
issues.quote: The third group was considered as a joint condition provided with both statistical and identifiable victim information.

issues.subcategory: factor coding conflates qualitatively different conditions
issues.description: Modeling identifiability as a three-level factor with levels identifiable, statistical, and joint may be statistically permissible but conceptually conflates separate vs joint evaluation and identifiability/statistics presence. This makes main effects difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability)

issues.description: Critical procedural information is delegated to a supplement/Qualtrics link rather than described in the manuscript: sequence of pages, timing, randomization, attention checks, donation question wording, feeling-item timing, and whether all participants saw all measures. This hampers replication and appraisal.
issues.quote: For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: Several links are placeholders ('<enter link here>') and some textual references are broken/duplicated. This obstructs access to materials, peer reviews, and presentation files and signals an incomplete manuscript.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here>

issues.description: Numerous references to supplementary sections are malformed or embedded in broken text, making it difficult to determine what is actually available. Essential methodological details should not depend on inaccessible or unclear supplements.
issues.quote: The experimental design can be retrieved from the supplementary under the section of  “Table of design”.Table of design

issues.description: There is no ethics approval or consent statement for human participants, despite planned online recruitment and potentially emotional charity-related stimuli. This is a standard reporting requirement.
issues.quote: [No ethics approval/consent statement provided in the manuscript]

issues.description: Compensation for actual participants is not specified, despite using MTurk and modifying the original incentive structure. Compensation influences participant motivation and donation responses and is necessary for replication assessment.
issues.quote: Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.subcategory: different motivational context from original payment structure
issues.description: The original participants donated from actual money received from a prior survey; the replication removes the earned-money context. This materially changes psychological ownership and sacrifice, likely affecting donation behavior and comparability.
issues.quote: Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: The manuscript simultaneously claims data collection was launched/completed and that methods/results will be updated after future data collection. This contradiction creates confusion about study status and undermines trust in the report.
issues.quote: Data collection for the experiment was launched at the start of the study period.

issues.description: The open-science section claims data collection was completed before analyses, but elsewhere the results are explicitly placeholders pending actual data collection. These statements cannot both be true.
issues.quote: data collection was completed before analyses

issues.description: The manuscript includes a student ID in the author details table. This is unnecessary personally identifying information and inappropriate for publication.
issues.quote: Student ID ... 3035682015

issues.description: A contributor (So Chi Liu) appears in the CRediT table but is not listed as an author or otherwise introduced, creating ambiguity about authorship and contribution reporting.
issues.quote: Role | Yik Chun Wong | Gilad Feldman | So Chi Liu

issues.description: The manuscript sometimes describes the identifiable victim effect as help toward a specific victim 'than to a group of statistical individuals', and elsewhere discusses 'physical helping behaviour' and 'donating responses' imprecisely. While not fatal, imprecise terminology complicates theoretical clarity.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is a phenomenon characterized by the human’s tendency to give out more aid to a specific victim than to a group of statistical individuals.

issues.description: There are multiple misspellings such as 'Solvic' instead of 'Slovic' and journal title inconsistencies. These errors reduce confidence in scholarship and can impede citation tracing.
issues.quote: Solvic, 2010

issues.description: The introduction makes normative claims about unfairness and inefficient resource allocation that go beyond what the cited studies establish and are not necessary for motivating a replication. This can bias framing.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation

issues.subcategory: correlation analyses likely underpowered/uncorrected and exploratory
issues.description: Multiple within-condition correlations between aggregated feelings and donation are reported, but no multiple-testing correction or clear preregistered rationale is provided. Given the altered design and placeholder data, these analyses add noise and are hard to interpret.
issues.quote: We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: No checks are reported for ANOVA assumptions (normality, homogeneity, independence), especially problematic given bounded/ordinal donation outcomes and possible unequal cell Ns. Without these, robustness of the tests is unclear.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA

issues.subcategory: cell sizes inconsistent with exclusions/randomization description
issues.description: Cell sizes are uneven but symmetric in a way suggestive of automatic generation rather than actual randomization. Since participants supposedly selected conditions, the basis of these cell counts is unexplained, further undermining interpretability.

Several hypotheses are vague or mismatched to analyses. For example, Hypothesis 4 says implicit learning reduces donations to an identifiable victim, but in the redesigned study this appears operationalized via a joint condition, which is not clearly isolated against an appropriate comparison. This ambiguity complicates testing and interpretation.
issues.quote: 4 (Interaction effect) | Implicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect reduces donations to an identifiable victim

issues.description: Although preregistration is linked, the manuscript does not summarize key preregistered decisions versus exploratory deviations. Given numerous design and analytic changes, explicit documentation of deviations is necessary.
issues.quote: Pre-registration on the Open Science Framework

issues.description: Several tables contain duplicated headers, malformed entries, and internal inconsistencies, which hinder interpretation and suggest insufficient manuscript preparation.
issues.quote:
|  | Hypothetical effect | Hypothetical effect
Hypothetical effect | Statistical testing | Original study | Replication
